title: Refinement changes your security boundary. Nobody announces when.
content:
Security teams treat refinement as oversight. It behaves like context inflation.

The mental model most teams use for AI calls looks like this: prompt goes in, model processes it, output comes out. Clean. Traceable. The security boundary is the prompt.

Refinement breaks this model in a specific way. Each refinement call adds the model's previous output back into the context. The model then processes not just your new instruction, but everything it said before. The security boundary is no longer your original prompt. It is your original prompt plus the entire history of what the model generated.

I want to be precise about what this means for security teams.

The first thing it changes is what the model has access to. In a single-turn call, the model sees exactly what you gave it. In a refinement loop, the model sees what you gave it plus what it generated. If that generation contains anything that could influence subsequent behavior — a tool call that left state, a context injection from an earlier turn, a latent instruction from the output — it persists.

The second thing it changes is auditability. In a single-turn call, you can reconstruct what the model was responding to. You have the prompt. In a refinement loop, the model is responding to a history. That history may not be fully recorded. When something goes wrong in production, the reconstruction question — what was the model actually acting on — becomes significantly harder.

The third thing is that the upgrade path is silent. Organizations that deploy AI systems often start with single-turn interactions and then add refinement or multi-turn capabilities. The security boundary they modeled was for the single-turn case. Nobody sends a notification when that boundary becomes invalid. The system works, the outputs look reasonable, and the attack surface quietly grows.

This is not an argument against refinement. It is an argument for modeling the attack surface correctly before adding it. The correct question is not whether refinement makes outputs better. It is what your model has access to at each step of the loop, and whether you have accounted for that in your trust model.
